content: Atopic diseases are among the most prevalent chronic conditions affecting children. Over the past three decades, there has been a notable increase in food anaphylaxis among young children, which is particularly concerning due to the limited availability of proven prevention strategies, aside from the timely introduction of allergenic foods such as peanuts and eggs. Differences in immune responses have been observed in vitro between infants vaccinated with the whole-cell pertussis (wP) vaccine and those vaccinated with the acellular pertussis (aP) vaccine. This prompted a systematic evaluation of the safety and potential allergy-preventive benefits of the wP vaccine to guide future clinical recommendations and research. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of wP vaccination compared to aP vaccination in early infancy for the prevention of atopic diseases in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, and grey literature, with the last search performed on September 7, 2020. The inclusion criteria for the study required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies of interventions (NRSIs) that reported on the occurrence of atopic diseases. Only RCTs were considered for assessing safety outcomes. Eligible studies needed to include children under 18 years of age who received their first dose of either wP (experimental intervention) or aP (comparator) before six months of age, with a minimum follow-up period of six months. Two independent reviewers screened the studies for eligibility, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias using standard Cochrane methods. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. The primary outcomes of interest were the diagnosis of IgE-mediated food allergy and all-cause serious adverse events (SAEs). Secondary outcomes included diagnoses of non-vaccine-associated anaphylaxis or urticaria, asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis, and encephalopathy. Due to the limited number of RCTs reporting on specific atopic outcomes, a broader outcome domain—cumulative incidence of atopic disease—was assessed as per the study protocol. Risk ratios (RR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used to summarize effect estimates, and safety data were pooled in meta-analyses using fixed-effect Mantel-Haenszel methods. The analysis included four studies reporting on atopic outcomes, encompassing a total of 7,333 children. A single trial provided uncertain evidence regarding whether wP vaccination influenced the risk of overall atopic disease (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.17) or asthma specifically (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.82) by 2.5 years of age. Three NRSIs were excluded from the narrative synthesis due to serious or critical risks of bias related to confounding and missing data. For safety outcomes, 21 studies involving 137,281 children were identified. Seven of these studies were judged to have a high risk of bias, while the remaining studies were deemed to have an unclear risk of bias. The pooled RR for all-cause SAEs was 0.94 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.15; I² = 0%; 15 studies, 38,072 children). Among every 1,000 children who received a first dose of wP, 11 experienced an SAE, compared to 12 children (95% CI 9 to 13) who received aP. The 95% CI for the risk difference ranged from three fewer to two more events per 1,000 children, and the certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate, downgraded one level due to imprecision. No cases of encephalopathy were reported following vaccination (95% CI for the risk difference: -5 to 12 per 100,000 children; seven primary series studies; 115,271 children). However, the certainty of the evidence for encephalopathy was judged as low, as this is a severe condition, and a clinically meaningful difference could not be excluded. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the effect of a first dose of wP vaccine administered early in infancy, compared to aP vaccine, on the risk of atopic diseases in children is of very low certainty. The incidence of all-cause SAEs was low for both wP and aP vaccines, and no cases of encephalopathy were reported. The certainty of the evidence was moderate for all-cause SAEs and low for encephalopathy. Future research should focus on using sensitive and specific clinical endpoints, particularly in populations with a high prevalence of IgE-mediated food allergies. Safety assessments should prioritize common vaccine reactions, parental acceptability, SAEs, and their potential relationship to the administered dose.
